newsitem.title: USA: Flight attendant takes stand in landmark Fla. tobacco trial.
newsitem.headline: Flight attendant takes stand in landmark Fla. tobacco trial.

text.p: Six years after suing the tobacco industry over secondhand cigarette smoke in airplanes, flight attendant Norma Broin took the witness stand Monday -- but was allowed to say little about how smoky passenger jets might have contributed to her lung cancer.

Broin's long-awaited testimony as the lead plaintiff in the landmark $5 billion lawsuit -- the first class action and first secondhand smoke suit against the tobacco industry to go to trial -- was punctuated by heated arguments over what she would be allowed to tell the jury.

Tobacco lawyers, who had argued unsuccessfully to bar her from the witness stand entirely, raised continual objections to her answers, and at one point the jury was led from the room for 30 minutes while the lawyers squabbled.

Broin's testimony came in the third month of the trial of Broin vs. Philip Morris et al, a class action filed on behalf of some 60,000 flight attendants who claim they were made sick by cigarette smoke while they worked on U.S. domestic flights.

Later in the day, lawyers read into the record testimony of a top tobacco industry research official who said he did not believe his organization, the Council for Tobacco Research, had subjected cigarettes or tobacco smoke to microscopic analysis.

Broin, a non-smoker and mother of two who is married to a Marine, was permitted to say little about her 1989 diagnosis with lung cancer and her membership in the Mormon Church, which forbids smoking. Broin's cancer is in remission.
Her testimony was the first in the trial from an airline industry employee who claims secondhand smoke gave her cancer.

Broin, 42, testified for about 60 minutes but was allowed to talk only in general terms about smoke in airplane passenger cabins prior to a 1990 ban on smoking on domestic flights, and her knowledge of the dangers of tobacco smoke.

"There was an incredible amount of dense, dense cigarette smoke," Broin, an American Airlines employee who began her career in 1976, said. "On occasion it would be so dense with cigarette smoke, even our smoking passengers would complain."
Passengers and flight attendants often would ask the captain to switch on the no-smoking sign to clear the air, she said.

Her testimony was restricted in part because of the manner in which Dade County Judge Robert Kaye structured the trial. The case is divided into two parts, with a first stage to decide generally whether secondhand smoke causes disease and if tobacco firms committed fraud, and a second stage in which flight attendants' individual claims of illness will be heard.
The arguments began when Broin's attorney, Stanley Rosenblatt, asked when she learned secondhand smoke could cause disease.

Public reliance on information disseminated by cigarette makers on the possible dangers of cigarette smoke is a critical issue in the trial. The plaintiffs maintain tobacco firms deliberately misled the public through false advertising and publications.
When the jury was escorted from the courtroom, tobacco lawyers argued that Broin should not be allowed to testify about how she might have relied on public information about the possible dangers.
"It's just totally prejudicial to allow her to testify on it in front of this jury," tobacco attorney High Whiting said.

Judge Robert Kaye determined that Broin could testify as to what she saw or knew based on what she had read, but barred her from saying anything about whether she relied on that information to make decisions.
When the jury returned, Rosenblatt asked Broin what she had known in the 1970s and 80s about secondhand smoke.
"Basically that it was very, very annoying. That it wouldn't cause me any serious health problems," she said. "That it was an irritant. It wasn't a serious threat."
When Rosenblatt asked her if smoking had not been banned on airplanes, whether she would be a flight attendant today, Broin replied "No," as tobacco lawyers rose to their feet to object.
"Don't sneak in answers," one industry lawyer said as voices rose and tempers flared.
"Don't start with me, either of you," Kaye admonished the attorneys.

Lawyers also read to the jury portions of a 199-page deposition taken in 1993 from Dr. Harmon McAllister, a vice president of the Council for Tobacco Research, an organization funded by cigarette makers to direct medical research on smoking.
McAllister said decades of research had found "risk factors" associated with smoking but no firm determination that smoking causes cancer and other diseases.
But asked if the council had conducted research in which cigarettes or tobacco smoke were subjected to microscopic analysis, McAllister said: "Not to my knowledge."
